description: A northern saga in the dark half of the year. Pinewood, fell and ice ringed by mountains; there are no shops, and everything is settled at the hall.

appearance.hallkeeper: Between you and the fire, and staying there until asked properly.
appearance.law-speaker: Reciting under her breath while you talk, and not losing her place.
appearance.skald: Half a verse in, watching to see whether you are worth the other half.
appearance.trapper: Furs to the chin, and a smell that arrived before he did.
appearance.fisher: Hands split at every knuckle, and entirely used to it.
appearance.herdsman: Counting something over your shoulder, twice.
appearance.housecarl: Armed indoors, which nobody here appears to find odd.
appearance.stone-keeper: Clearing snow off a carving that is beyond reading anyway.
appearance.boatwright: Steaming a plank, and will not leave it for you.
appearance.weaver: At the loom with the shutters closed against the cold.
appearance.cooper: Hands pale with shavings, a half-hooped barrel between the knees.

talksAbout.law-speaker: what was settled at the last thing, and who has not abided by it
talksAbout.skald: the winter, the dead, and which of the two is longer
talksAbout.hallkeeper: who is drinking on credit, and how much of it there is
talksAbout.trapper: the trapline, the wolves, and what the wolves have been doing lately
talksAbout.stone-keeper: the waystones, and the road they are supposed to mark
talksAbout.herdsman: the fodder, the frost, and how far it is to spring
talksAbout.housecarl: the watch, and the ships that came up the fjord in the autumn

lore.title: The Second Winter
lore.premise: The summer failed and did not come back, and the halls have been eating their seed corn since the equinox. The waystones on the high road have started being found turned to face the wrong way.
lore.era: the winter that has lasted two years
lore.tone: hard, plainspoken, and superstitious about it
deities: the Lady of the Deep Water

ambient: Your breath goes ahead of you and hangs there.
The snow has gone blue, which means the light is nearly finished for today.
Something crossed here on four feet, unhurried, since the last fall.
The pines take the wind and give back a sound like water.
There is a cairn off the track, and somebody has kept the snow off it.

hall: Sweet, strong, and poured for guests before it is asked for.
Undyed wool, wound on a shaved stick.
Notched, split, and half of it kept elsewhere.
house: Fox and hare, badly cured but warm.
Split, hung, and hard as a board.
barn: In a stoppered horn. It is for the lamps, mostly.
smithy: Dug out of the fen, and half of it is not iron.
A sack of it, light as nothing.
warehouse: Heavy, and worth more than it looks.
ruin: Warm to the hand before it should be.
shrine: Left in the lee of the stone, and not taken.

inn: Sweet, strong, and it arrives whether or not you asked.
Fox and hare. Warm rather than fine.
Split, hung, and hard as a board.
In a stoppered horn, for a lamp or a boot.
Nearer than a stranger is usually given.
smithy: Bog iron, and better than that sounds.
Meant for wood. It would do for other things.
A twist of them, clenched square.
Iron spikes on a strap, for the fell in the wrong month.
stable: Enough for a week on the road.

conifer: Amber beads, tacky even in this cold.
Dead branches from under the skirt of a pine, and dry.
marsh: Rust-red lumps, dug out with the hands.
Late, few, and the best thing on the fell.
bush: Black, watery, and better than nothing.
snow: It will not last, and it knows it.
Somebody's snare, and they are not here to argue.
rock: It takes a hard edge and a harder spark.
Scraped off in flakes. It will boil down into something.
deadTree: Split from a trunk dead long enough to be dry.
stump: Weeping still, out of a cut made years ago.
